overview: Zanzibar’s history includes Swahili communities, Omani royal government and connections with India, Arabia and Europe. Stone Town’s streets and buildings preserve that mixture. Palace life, shopkeeping and plantation labour offer very different views of the same society.

periods.title: Omani rule in an older trading settlement
periods.summary: Omani forces established a fort around earlier Portuguese structures near the end of the seventeenth century. Archaeology also reaches much earlier Swahili occupation. The map’s 1715 starting point is not the birth of Zanzibar’s communities or its later separate sultanate.

periods.title: A royal court on the island
periods.summary: Sultan Said established his court in Zanzibar during the 1830s. Merchants and royal buildings helped reshape the town. This court still belonged to a wider realm connecting Zanzibar with Oman.

periods.title: A divided royal inheritance
periods.summary: Said’s death in 1856 divided his realm between heirs. Zanzibar’s separation from Muscat was subsequently settled in 1861.

periods.title: A separate sultanate
periods.summary: Zanzibar became a separate sultanate in 1861. Its earlier Omani connections should not be confused with an independent Zanzibar state already existing at the map’s first date.

periods.title: The British protectorate
periods.summary: In 1890 the sultan accepted British protection and British control of foreign relations. The sultanate continued, with its freedom of action constrained by imperial power.

periods.title: Abolition under the protectorate
periods.summary: Slavery was legally abolished in Zanzibar in 1897. This political period continued beyond the map’s endpoint in 1914; that map boundary is not the date the sultanate ended.

periods.title: A short independent monarchy
periods.summary: The protectorate ended on 10 December 1963. Zanzibar briefly continued as an independent state under its sultan before revolution the following month.

periods.title: Revolution, union and continuing communities
periods.summary: The revolution of 12 January 1964 overthrew the monarchy. On 26 April, Zanzibar united with Tanganyika in the country later called Tanzania. Zanzibar retained distinct institutions, including its own later House of Representatives.

sections.title: A house around a patch of sky

items.text: Stone Town’s historic houses often used coral limestone, mangrove timber and lime mortar. Many larger houses arranged long, narrow rooms around an open courtyard. The building’s shape helped organise domestic space around that opening. A handsome carved entrance belonged to a practical building, not merely a decorative front.

The town also included simpler single-storey Swahili houses and Indian bazaar buildings centred on a duka, or shop. Those differences matter: a palace cannot stand in for everybody’s home. Shop spaces are reminders that urban life involved buying, selling and making a living as well as royal ceremonies.

sections.title: What was here before the fort?

items.text: Excavations in the Old Fort’s western courtyard in 2017 and 2018 traced occupation back to an eleventh-century Swahili settlement beside the beach. Imported ceramics helped researchers investigate long connections with the Gulf. A broken pot can reveal a trading relationship, although it cannot by itself tell us the language or birthplace of its owner.

The same site later held a Portuguese trading establishment and an Augustinian mission. Omani builders reused the church within a square fort; nineteenth-century expansion produced two courtyards. A place can preserve several political histories in its walls. The present fort therefore does not represent one untouched building from a single moment.

sections.title: Someone drew boats on the wall

items.text: Researchers recorded ship drawings scratched into dry plaster at the Old Fort, especially inside its southwestern tower and along its ramparts. Hulls, masts and rigging appear in the marks. Building history and vessel types suggest a mid- to late-nineteenth-century date. The drawings are material traces of somebody looking closely at ships.
Who held the sharp point? The researchers suggest members of the fort’s garrison, who had access to these spaces and could see shipping nearby. Their makers remain unidentified.

sections.title: Royal plumbing, including the less glamorous part

items.text: At Mtoni palace, researchers excavated a water channel in 2008. Their architectural study connects the palace’s water supply with a nineteenth-century aqueduct from the Chem Chem spring. This is practical evidence behind a grand residence: bringing water to the household required planned structures, not just a good view of the sea.

Mtoni’s bathing complex included cold-water bathhouses and a separate heated bath. The latter had cold, warm and hot rooms with a boiler. These were facilities of a royal household, not evidence that everyone in Zanzibar had such a bathroom. Even within the palace, different bathing arrangements served different residents.

The cold-water bathhouses also had latrines that were emptied through hatches at the rear. Channels ran beneath the bathing complex, while raised back rooms accommodated washing and toilet use. Royal architecture needed arrangements for waste as well as impressive reception rooms. Somebody still had to do the emptying.

Princess Salme, later known as Emily Ruete, remembered lessons in the royal household on an open veranda. Children used bamboo pens, homemade ink and cleaned camel shoulder blades as writing surfaces. Enslaved people prepared the bones. This was her recollection of an elite nineteenth-century childhood, not a description of every Zanzibar school.

Before lessons, Salme recalled children wrestling and climbing a balustrade. A lookout coughed when the teacher approached, and everybody hurried to sit down. The account comes from memory, but the scene is wonderfully recognisable: an unusually well-coordinated effort to look as though absolutely nothing had been happening.

In her household, girls were taught reading while boys also learned writing. Salme secretly copied characters onto a bone, then learned more with help from an enslaved writing teacher. Her story records both a girl pursuing an excluded skill and knowledge held by a person whose own freedom was denied.

sections.title: A bench, a floor and the work behind cloves

items.text: At the nineteenth-century plantation site of Mgoli on Pemba, a 2004 excavation uncovered a partly dismantled baraza, a bench outside a stone house. Beside it lay a packed-rubble floor interpreted as a place for drying cloves. A working floor at Bweni and local residents’ knowledge supported that interpretation.

Freshly picked cloves had to dry before export, and enslaved workers supplied the plantation labour. Croucher suggests that a bench beside the drying area could let owners watch that work while also serving as a social space. The bench and floor were excavated; this explanation of surveillance is an interpretation of their position.

Merchant Tharia Topan commissioned the building later called the Old Dispensary; its foundation stone was laid in 1887. After his death, his wife Janbai oversaw the project, but the completed building still needed money for equipment and staff. A fine building alone did not make a working clinic. It began operating under new ownership in 1900.

The early dispensary treated patients in three ground-floor rooms used for consultations, treatment and pharmacy services. Apartments occupied the upper floors. After later closure and restoration, the building returned to healthcare use as the Aga Khan Health Centre. Its history joins medical work, housing and the challenge of adapting an old building to a new purpose.

ending.text: The sultanate ended in the revolution of 12 January 1964, which replaced the monarchy with a republic. Zanzibar united with Tanganyika on 26 April that year. Its communities continued, and Zanzibar later developed its own House of Representatives within Tanzania. The map’s endpoint in 1914 is not this political ending.
